title: The golden calf (Exodus 32)
hook: they melt their earrings into a god they can see

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Decalogue, which opens with a rescue, not a rule. Your line was freedom first, then the law.

Moses has been up the mountain for forty days. No word, just a cloud on the summit and silence. Down in the camp, people start talking. Maybe he's dead. And the God he talks to is invisible, up there in the smoke. So they go to Aaron, Moses's brother, the one left in charge: make us gods to go before us. As for this Moses, we don't know what happened to him. And Aaron says: bring me your gold earrings.
screen: `FORTY DAYS. NO MOSES.` → `MAKE US GODS.` → `BRING ME YOUR EARRINGS.`

segments.voice: First, the calf. Aaron melts the gold and shapes a young bull, and the people say, "These are thy gods, O Israel, that have brought thee out of the land of Egypt." Then Aaron builds an altar and announces a feast of the Lord, using God's own name. That's the twist. They aren't exactly walking away from the God who rescued them. They're trying to make that God visible, portable, controllable. Second, the excuse. When Moses comes down, sees the dancing and smashes the tablets, Aaron says, more or less: they gave me gold, I threw it in the fire, and out came this calf. It's what a parent might hear from a child standing next to a broken vase. Third, the word. Idol comes from the Greek eidolon, an image, even a phantom: something that looks like the real thing and isn't. The Catechism widens it. Idolatry isn't only about statues: a person commits idolatry whenever they honor a created thing in place of God, and it lists power, pleasure, money, race, the state. Fourth, the obvious question. Catholic churches are full of statues and icons. Are those idols? The Catholic and Orthodox answer comes from a council at Nicaea in 787: the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows. In Catholic teaching, the prayer goes to the person, not the plaster. Some Protestant churches, reading the same commandment, keep their walls plain. The real test in Exodus 32 isn't whether there's gold in the room. It's what the people let take God's place.
screen: `THESE ARE THY GODS, O ISRAEL.` · `THIS CALF CAME OUT.` · `EIDOLON: AN IMAGE, A PHANTOM.` · `WHAT TAKES GOD'S PLACE?`

segments.voice: Ask yourself honestly: what do I check first in the morning, what do I most fear losing, where does my money go when it's tight? Some answers will be good things, work, family, health, and the calf was made of good gold, too; just notice which one sits in the center, and whether that's where you want it. If you pray, set that thing before God and ask for the right order; if not, simply hold the question.
Idol. From Greek eidolon, an image. Anything, golden or not, that a person lets take the place of God. Today's word.
Your line: what are you worshiping. Good things can still sit in the wrong place. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: The Catechism teaches that idolatry includes putting power, pleasure, money or any created thing in God's place, and that venerating holy images is not idolatry, because the honor passes to the person the image represents.

chat.says: If nobody bows to gold statues anymore, is idolatry even a thing now?
options: Yes: an idol is anything you let take God's place, like money, power or pleasure.
Not really; idolatry only meant bowing to statues, and that has mostly died out.
Only for people who still keep carved images of other gods at home.
